clue.text: Good knight with lot lost, hit on the field

indicators.note: lost tells us the word lot drops out of the knight's name

parts.note: Sir Lancelot is the Arthurian knight of the Round Table
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket report: a good batsman, a knight even, out of luck but still striking the ball on the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lot lost' reads like bad luck but is an instruction to the knight's name. A glance is a cricket stroke deflecting the ball fine off the bat's face.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a glance is a deft deflecting stroke, a way of hitting the ball on the field of play.

clue.text: Not all bowling at Edgbaston will get a wicket?

indicators.note: Not all says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A cricket question: will every delivery at Edgbaston, the Birmingham Test ground, take a wicket?
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition 'will get a wicket' is a verb phrase; only 'a wicket' is a noun to swap for the answer, so 'will get' is link. A wicket is also a small gate.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides its cricket sense, a wicket is a small door or gate, often set within a larger one.

clue.text: First of all, horses must be given numbers

indicators.note: takes just the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: mounts are horses for riding

explanation.surface: An instruction that before anything else the horses need numbers, as at a race.
explanation.definitionFit: Amounts and numbers are both quantities or totals.

clue.text: Conservative meeting leading bosses — are there skeletons hiding here?

parts.note: up means ahead, as in a team two goals up
the board of directors runs a company

explanation.surface: A Tory meets top executives, and we wonder what scandals they are concealing.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the idiom 'a skeleton in the cupboard', a hidden scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: Family secrets are proverbially skeletons in the closet, so this storage space is where they lurk.

clue.text: Man of class, maybe English, with old money and gold

parts.note: the ducat was a gold coin of old European currency
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Describes a well-to-do Englishman with old family money and gold in the vaults.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man of class' suggests an aristocrat, but the class is a schoolroom one; 'maybe' marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacher stands in front of a class, so a schoolmaster is one example of this person.

clue.text: The driving idea originally conjured up for supposed royal prerogative

indicators.note: conjured suggests magic transformation, so the letters are rearranged
takes just the initial letter of idea

explanation.surface: The motivating notion first summoned up to justify a monarch's claimed privilege.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conjured up' rearranges THE DRIVING plus I, the first letter of 'idea'.
explanation.definitionFit: The doctrine held kings answerable only to God, a claimed sovereign entitlement now discredited.

clue.text: Open Voltaire's work — don't close it

indicators.note: means leave off the final letter of the title

parts.note: Candide is Voltaire's satirical novel

explanation.surface: An instruction to open a copy of Voltaire's book and not shut it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open' looks like a verb about the book but is the adjective meaning frank.
explanation.definitionFit: Candid and open both describe frank, honest speech with nothing concealed.

clue.text: Pound troy — half-forgotten weight

indicators.note: the second half of the word is dropped, keeping the first

parts.note: the ounce is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A note on measures: pound troy, a weight system half-forgotten today.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like the unit but is the verb to beat soundly.
explanation.definitionFit: To trounce is to defeat heavily or thrash, as one might pound an opponent.

clue.text: Soldier keeps to rules I lay down

indicators.note: holding the word to inside the soldier

parts.note: a regular is a professional soldier in the standing army

explanation.surface: A soldier sticks to the regulations I set out.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks in the answer's own voice: one who lays down rules.
explanation.definitionFit: A regulator is an official body or person that sets and enforces rules.

clue.text: Performers walk in the auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is where things are heard, so this signals a word that sounds the same

parts.note: to troop is to walk along together in a body

explanation.surface: Actors make their way through the theatre seating, perhaps as part of an immersive show.
explanation.walkthrough: TROOP and TROUPE are pronounced the same; the auditorium fits the theatre picture while signalling the homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: A troupe is a company of touring actors, dancers or other entertainers.

clue.text: Service just the same, no good

parts.note: even so means nevertheless, just the same

explanation.surface: A grumble that a church service is the same as ever and no good.
explanation.definitionFit: Evensong is the Anglican evening prayer service, sung in many cathedrals.

clue.text: Bohemian learner joining a foreign religious house on holy island

parts.note: un is French for a
a convent is a house of nuns
Iona is the Scottish island where St Columba founded his monastery
L is the learner plate abbreviation

explanation.surface: A free-spirited novice joins an overseas nunnery on a sacred isle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bohemian' looks like a nationality but means free-living; IONA is a Hebridean island off western Scotland, a cradle of Celtic Christianity.
explanation.definitionFit: A bohemian lives an artistic life outside conventional social rules, hence unorthodox.

clue.text: Most in French resort upset during holiday? One should minimise health risk

indicators.note: puts the letters inside the holiday word

parts.note: vacation is a holiday

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the letters upside down, reading backwards
most of the word, losing its last letter

parts.note: Nice is a resort on the French Riviera

explanation.surface: Most people at a Riviera resort fall ill on holiday, so get your jabs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most' trims the resort's last letter, 'upset' reads the rest backwards (up the column), and 'during' sets it in the holiday word. 'upset' pretends to mean tummy trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A vaccination is a jab that protects against disease, so it reduces the danger of infection.

clue.text: Unhappy fellow 'gutted', we hear? Support found in church

indicators.note: says the phrase is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a misery is a gloomy person, and cored means gutted like an apple

explanation.surface: A miserable man, devastated, finds comfort in church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutted' looks like British slang for upset, but here it is CORED. Said together, MISERY CORED sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A misericord is a ledge under a hinged choir seat that props up a standing worshipper.

clue.text: Skill needing to keep working in male community

indicators.note: holding the word for working inside the skill

parts.note: mastery is great skill
on means operating or working

explanation.surface: A craft that needs ongoing practice within a group of men.
explanation.definitionFit: A monastery is a house where a community of monks live together.

clue.text: Trench in meadow ending with silt

parts.note: lea is a poetic word for a meadow

indicators.note: takes only the last letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A ditch in a field whose far end is clogged with silt.
explanation.definitionFit: A leat is an open watercourse or channel dug to carry water to a mill.

clue.text: Cut back on iron?

parts.note: to cut back on something is to reduce it, and an iron takes the creases out of a garment

explanation.surface: Should I reduce my iron intake?
explanation.walkthrough: 'iron' suggests dietary iron, but it is the household appliance that removes creases: read as DE-CREASE.
explanation.definitionFit: To reduce or lessen something is to make it smaller, and pressing a shirt literally takes the creases out.

clue.text: Only off when mad dogs go out?

definitions.text: Only off when mad dogs go out?

parts.words: Only off when mad dogs go out?
parts.note: Noel Coward's song says only mad dogs and Englishmen go out in the midday sun, and the word reads the same off either end

explanation.surface: A riddle about the one time crazed hounds venture out.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel Coward's song 'Mad Dogs and Englishmen' says they go out in the midday sun; 'Only off' hints that the word is NO + ON, which is its own reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Midday is twelve o'clock in the day, the hour of the song's blazing sun.

clue.text: Top clue cunningly constructed? This one is word-wise!

indicators.note: something built with cunning is cleverly reworked, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A setter boasting that this clue is a cleverly made top-notch one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cunningly constructed' rearranges TOP CLUE. The definition is a quirky self-reference to the answer's meaning of eightfold.
explanation.definitionFit: Octuple means eightfold, consisting of eight parts, a term Pasquale playfully applies to the clue itself.

clue.text: Grander lie broadcast by chief villain

indicators.note: scattered widely, so the letters are spread out and rearranged

explanation.surface: A bigger falsehood spread by the arch-villain over the airwaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' rearranges the letters of GRANDER LIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringleader heads a gang or plot, the principal wrongdoer among a group.

clue.text: Party with yob carrying drug to distribute

parts.note: a do is a party

indicators.note: holding the drug inside the yob

parts.note: a lout is a boorish yob
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A party where a thug carries drugs to hand round.
explanation.definitionFit: To dole out is to hand round or share out portions.

clue.text: One with fifty occupying beach, say, in Ibiza?

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: the numeral sits inside the beach word

parts.note: sand covers a beach and stands for it
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A lone tourist with fifty others crowding a beach on Ibiza.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks Ibiza as an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibiza is one of the Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean, an example of land surrounded by sea.

clue.text: One left in workplace after final day is all right

indicators.note: puts the building after the day

parts.note: Saturday, abbreviated SAT, is traditionally the last day of the week

indicators.note: places one thing within the word for workplace

parts.note: a factory is a place of work
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone stays behind at the factory after the last day, and that's fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts IL inside the workplace word; 'after' places that after the day; 'final day' is Saturday as the week's end.
explanation.definitionFit: Satisfactorily means acceptably or adequately, in a way that passes muster.

clue.text: What's loud has listener showing anxiety

parts.note: F is forte, the musical direction for loud
the ear is the organ of hearing

explanation.surface: Something loud makes a listener anxious.
explanation.definitionFit: Fear and anxiety are both feelings of dread or apprehension.

clue.text: Vehement cheat — PM, I fancy

indicators.note: fancy as a verb means imagine, and here invites an imaginative rearrangement

explanation.surface: A strong accusation: the Prime Minister is a cheat, I reckon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' rearranges CHEAT PM I; 'I fancy' looks like a throwaway aside but the I is part of the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Vehement and emphatic both describe speech delivered with force and conviction.

clue.text: Downtrodden worker keeping a promise

indicators.note: holding the letter inside the worker

parts.note: prole, from proletarian, is a working-class labourer

explanation.surface: An oppressed labourer holding onto a pledge.
explanation.definitionFit: Parole is word of honour, a prisoner's pledge given in exchange for early release.

clue.text: Lie dying, sadly giving up

indicators.note: something done sadly goes wrong, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A deathbed scene: lying there dying, giving up the fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges LIE DYING.
explanation.definitionFit: Yielding is surrendering or submitting, so it means conceding or surrendering ground.

clue.text: Harry is safe — son's in hiding

indicators.note: concealed within the word for safe

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe

explanation.surface: Prince Harry is safe, his son tucked away out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like a name but is the verb; a peter is underworld slang for a safe.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry is to harass persistently, the same as to badger or nag.
